facts.text: Allergic diseases such as hay fever and asthma have become much more common over recent decades, especially in wealthy countries.
In 1989, British doctor David Strachan reported that hay fever was less common in children with more older siblings.
Strachan used data on thousands of British children born in 1958.
He suggested that infections spread in large families might protect against allergy, and that smaller families and cleaner homes reduced them.
His idea became known as the hygiene hypothesis.
Children raised on traditional farms with animals have less asthma; Amish farm children had far less than Hutterite children on industrial farms.
Researchers now stress regular contact with a wide range of harmless microbes, rather than infection itself, as what trains the immune system.
Experts argue the term hygiene hypothesis is misleading, because it can lead people to neglect hygiene that prevents infection.
There is no good evidence that everyday hygiene such as handwashing is responsible for the change in microbial exposure; targeted hygiene is still needed.
The rise in allergy is thought to have several causes, including genes, air pollution and diet.
